Bennington.wildlife_intro:
Bennington's calls come from the meeting of a historic town and two mountain ranges. Bats roost in the big attics of Old Bennington and in older downtown homes, raccoons and squirrels work the mature street trees and mill-era housing along the Walloomsac, and skunks, woodchucks, and porcupines are routine on the rural edges. North Bennington's millpond and older buildings add their own share of raccoon and bat work.

Cold winters send mice and squirrels inside early here, and homes that sit quiet between visits need checking before fall. Spring brings denning raccoons in chimneys and skunks under porches, while summer bat colonies are handled by exclusion only — one-way doors in spring and late August through fall, proofing from December through March, and no work that strands flightless pups. Our crew lives with these seasons and will tell you honestly what can be done now and what should wait.

faqs.q: Are bats a problem in Old Bennington's historic homes?
faqs.a: They can be. Tall attics, slate roofs, and small gaps at chimneys and eaves give bats exactly the warm, quiet roost they look for, and colonies return to the same house summer after summer. The fix is careful proofing of every other opening plus one-way doors at the exits, timed outside the pup season. Our crew is used to working gently on historic fabric.

Manchester.wildlife_intro:
Manchester's biggest wildlife driver is the second home. Houses that sit empty for weeks give bats, squirrels, mice, and raccoons time to move in unnoticed, and the Battenkill valley and Equinox slopes keep a healthy population right at the tree line. Village homes see the usual attic squirrels and chimney raccoons, while larger homes and inns on the edges deal with bat colonies, porcupines at outbuildings, and woodchucks in the gardens.

Our crew checks many Manchester homes at opening and closing, because mud season and early winter are when quiet houses are most vulnerable. A home closed up in fall can hold a winter's worth of mouse damage by spring, and a summer bat colony needs exclusion timed for spring or late August through November, never while pups cannot fly. If your place sits empty part of the year, call us for a proofing inspection before you leave.

faqs.q: My Manchester home is empty for months at a time. How do I keep animals out?
faqs.a: Proofing is the answer — sealing roofline gaps, screening chimneys and vents, and closing foundation openings while the house is occupied and can be checked. Our crew can inspect before you close up, remove anything already inside, and seal the building so winter mice and spring raccoons find no way in. It is far cheaper than cleaning up after a season inside.

Pownal.wildlife_intro:
Pownal is quiet valley country where most calls come from farmhouses and rural homes rather than dense neighborhoods. Raccoons and skunks get into barns, chicken coops, and under porches, porcupines chew sheds and camps in the woods, and bats summer in older farmhouse attics and big barns. Woodchucks work the Hoosic flats, and squirrels and mice are a constant in homes backed up against Green Mountain and Taconic forest.

Winter is hard and long in the valley, so fall proofing matters — once snow is on the ground, animals already inside stay inside. Spring brings skunks and raccoons raising young under buildings, and summer bat work follows the exclusion-only rule, with one-way doors in spring and late summer through fall and full proofing in winter. Vermont prohibits relocating furbearers, so our crew will explain the lawful removal options for your situation when you call.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Pownal, VT?
faqs.a: It depends on the species, how the animal got in, and how much proofing or cleanup the building needs, so we do not quote a firm price before seeing the job. After an inspection, our crew can explain the options and the cost for your home or camp in Pownal, with no pressure to go ahead.

faqs.q: Can you relocate a skunk or raccoon from my Pownal property?
faqs.a: No — Vermont prohibits relocating furbearers, and moving an animal often just spreads disease and dumps the problem on someone else. What our crew can do is remove the animal lawfully under a valid Vermont trapping license where trapping is needed, exclude it from the building with one-way methods where that fits, and proof your home so the next animal cannot move in.

Dorset.wildlife_intro:
Dorset mixes a picture-book village with deep woods on three sides, and wildlife moves freely between them. Squirrels and bats are the main attic calls in the village's older homes, raccoons work barns and chimneys along both valleys, and porcupines are a persistent problem at camps, sheds, and second homes on the Equinox and Green Peak roads. Woodchucks favor the open farm ground in the Mettawee valley and around the village green.

Many Dorset homes are seasonal, and a quiet house over a long winter invites mice, squirrels, and porcupines to settle in. Our crew often opens a house in spring to find a season of gnawing or a bat colony returning to a familiar attic — bat exclusion is timed for spring or late August through November with one-way doors, and winter is for proofing, never for sealing in a colony. Call us before you close up and we will make the house hard to enter.

faqs.q: How much does wildlife removal cost in Dorset, VT?

faqs.q: Are porcupines a serious problem for Dorset camps and second homes?
faqs.a: Yes, they are one of the most damaging quiet-season animals here. A porcupine can gnaw siding, deck boards, and outhouse and shed wood all winter for the salt in it, and the damage is often discovered months later. Our crew can remove the animal and advise on shielding vulnerable wood and clearing salt sources, which together stop repeat visits.
